intro: The SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam held on 26 October 2026 was conducted in three shifts. Partial analyses have been published for each shift, offering a limited view that still requires further corroboration. Unofficial figures suggest that candidates who attempted between roughly 56 and 74 questions performed relatively well, but SSC normalises scores across shifts, so direct comparison is not definitive. Subject‑wise feedback indicates English ranged from easy to moderate, while reasoning, general awareness and quantitative aptitude varied from moderate to difficult. All numbers are unofficial and should be treated as indicative only.

faqs.q: What was the overall difficulty level reported for the 26 October 2026 SSC CGL Tier 1 exam?
faqs.a: The partial analysis indicates that Shift 1 was reported as moderate, Shift 2 as easy to moderate, and Shift 3 as moderate to difficult overall.

faqs.q: How many questions were candidates reported to have attempted successfully on 26 October 2026?
faqs.a: Unofficial ranges suggest that candidates attempted well on about 62–68 questions in Shift 1, 68–74 questions in Shift 2, and 56–64 questions in Shift 3. These figures are not official and are provided only as an indication.

faqs.q: Which subjects were considered easier or harder on 26 October 2026?
faqs.a: English was generally described as easy to moderate across the shifts. Reasoning was easy to moderate in Shift 2 and moderate in the others. General awareness varied from moderate to difficult, and quantitative aptitude ranged from moderate to difficult.

faqs.q: What topics were most frequently mentioned in the analysis for 26 October 2026?
faqs.a: Candidates repeatedly highlighted syllogism, puzzles, seating‑arrangement questions, current‑affairs items, arithmetic data‑interpretation, and reading‑comprehension passages across all three shifts.

faqs.q: How reliable is the analysis for the 26 October 2026 shifts?
faqs.a: All three shifts have a status of partial, meaning only a limited review is available and it needs further corroboration. The figures quoted are unofficial, and SSC normalises scores across shifts, so the analysis should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.
